title: Columbus Motherful Nonprofit Closes on Far East Side Site for Co-Housing
author: CRE News Staff
excerpt: Columbus nonprofit Motherful has closed on a 2-acre site at 100 Noe Bixby Rd. in Far East Columbus, planning 18 bedrooms of affordable co-housing for single mothers and their families.

body:
Motherful, a Columbus nonprofit collective founded in 2018 to support single mothers, has closed on a two-acre property at 100 Noe Bixby Road in Far East Columbus for a co-housing development. The four-building project will provide 18 bedrooms of affordable, cooperative housing for roughly 10 families, with shared childcare support, kitchen, and community resources.

## A Different Kind of Affordable Housing Model

Most affordable housing development in Columbus advances through the state's Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program, which requires developers, equity investors, and competitive rounds administered by the Ohio Housing Finance Agency. Motherful's Noe Bixby project follows a different path: the organization owns the property directly and is advancing the renovation without a public tax-credit allocation.

Co-housing is a model in which residents have private space but share common areas and, often, governance. Motherful's version is oriented around shared support for single mothers: a common kitchen and pantry, on-site childcare support, gardens and play areas, and expectations of shared labor — meal preparation rotations, maintenance, and community upkeep. [Columbus Underground reported](https://columbusunderground.com/local-group-moving-forward-with-co-housing-project-for-single-mothers-bw1/) the property close and described the development as the first co-housing community of this kind Motherful has pursued.

## The Site: 100 Noe Bixby Road

100 Noe Bixby Road sits in Far East Columbus, east of I-270 near the Hamilton Road and Eastland area. The zip code (43232) covers a part of the city that has attracted less concentrated development investment than corridors like the Near East Side and South Side, where LIHTC projects, major healthcare acquisitions, and nonprofit land purchases have been more active over the past several years — CREN has previously covered [Nationwide Children's $7.6M East Main acquisition](/blog/nationwide-children-s-buys-7-6m-east-main-street-block-no-plans-yet) and [the $7M Mt. Vernon Avenue Phase 1 rebuild](/blog/2026-09-20-columbus-mt-vernon-avenue-7m-rebuild-king-lincoln-bronzeville) on the Near East Side.

The four buildings on the property include one designated as Motherful's organizational headquarters and three renovated for residential use. No permit filing for the renovation was found in Columbus Building and Zoning Services records at the time of this report, and no construction timeline or budget has been made public.

## Three Features That Make This Project Unusual

**Direct nonprofit ownership.** Motherful bought the property rather than partnering with a for-profit developer. That structure gives the organization long-term control over who lives there and how the community operates — but it also places capital and maintenance responsibility entirely on the nonprofit, without the legal and financial protections that a developer partnership or public subsidy structure would carry.

**Services embedded in the housing itself.** On-site childcare support is built into the model rather than contracted separately or left to individual residents. [NBC4 reported](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/columbus/nonprofit-aims-to-help-single-mothers-avoid-loneliness/) on the organization's mission to address the specific isolation that single mothers experience, noting that Motherful has grown to roughly 2,000 members in the Columbus area. The shared kitchen, pantry, and common space are designed around that need, not retrofitted into a standard multifamily floor plan.

**Shared governance, not a conventional tenancy.** Residents participate in collective decision-making and mutual aid. That arrangement is uncommon in publicly funded affordable housing and carries a different risk profile: if the organization encounters financial or operational difficulties, residents' protections differ from those in a standard landlord-tenant relationship. The nature of occupancy agreements at the Noe Bixby site has not been publicly described.

## What This Means for Far East Columbus

Far East Columbus — the Eastland and Hamilton Road corridor east of I-270 — has seen uneven investment in the current development cycle. The Motherful project is small (18 bedrooms, roughly 10 families), but it represents nonprofit-owned property control in a zip code that has fewer institutional anchors than the inner-ring neighborhoods closer to downtown. The co-housing model, if it succeeds, could demonstrate a replicable structure for community-led affordable housing that does not depend on competitive state credit rounds.

The Columbus City Council approved a [$500 million Housing Bond in July 2026](/blog/columbus-begins-deploying-500-million-housing-bond) that is beginning to flow into the market. Whether co-housing projects like Motherful's can access any portion of that funding — or whether the city's bond structure is oriented primarily toward larger LIHTC and multifamily developments — has not been addressed in any public documentation reviewed for this story.

## What to Watch

The first public checkpoint will be a permit filing with Columbus Building and Zoning Services, which is the step that triggers formal city review. Given the project's size, permits are likely administrative rather than contested — but any variance request or neighborhood objection would produce a public hearing. [Motherful's website](https://www.motherful.org/motherful-housing) describes the project's vision without a completion date. The organization has not responded to a request for comment on the renovation timeline or budget; CREN will update this story when that information becomes available.
